prompt: Deleted customer rows reappear after a Cassandra replica returns from a five-day outage. The table's deletion grace is four days, the latest scheduled repair is green globally, one token range was skipped, and compaction ran during the outage. Read consistency is ONE and clocks differ by 90 seconds. Diagnose, contain, recover and prevent recurrence without assuming the largest timestamp is business truth.
directAnswer: Declare a correctness and possible privacy incident. Stop aggressive compaction/purge, broad repair, topology movement and repeated deletes. Bind affected table, partition keys, tokens, replicas, deletion mutation timestamps, source business operation IDs, outage interval, grace configuration, skipped repair range, SSTables/compaction and client/coordinator clocks. Five-day outage exceeded four-day grace; the affected range missed repair, so healthy replicas could purge tombstones while the returning replica retained live values. Consistency ONE can expose one replica, and 90-second skew can distort last-write-wins ordering, but the exact scope still needs proof. Isolate the stale replica or affected reads under reviewed procedure, establish deletion authority from the source business record, then use the supported version-specific scoped reconciliation/repair or controlled rewrite with adequate headroom. Verify absence on every replica and through the consumer. Prevent with per-range—not global—repair age/coverage, outage plus schedule plus duration plus margin below grace, clock monitoring, deletion drills, guarded compaction and idempotent deletion identity.
foundation: A deletion is replicated timestamped evidence. If a replica misses that evidence and surviving tombstones are purged before convergence, stale live data can return. Global job green and cluster averages do not prove range coverage.
reasoningSteps: Declare correctness/privacy impact and freeze evidence-changing work.
Bind keys, tokens, replicas, timestamps, clocks and business authority.
Compare five-day outage to four-day grace.
Find skipped repair range behind misleading global green.
Treat consistency ONE as exposure path, not root cause alone.
Isolate stale serving and calculate recovery headroom.
Restore authoritative deletion through scoped supported reconciliation.
Verify every replica and consumer state.
Repair per-range monitoring, horizon policy and clock discipline.
Rehearse deletion and recovery with cleanup evidence.
seniorAnswer: This is deletion-safety failure until disproven. Five days offline exceeds four-day grace, the relevant range missed repair, and compaction may have purged tombstones. I freeze purge and topology work, isolate stale service, preserve timestamps/repair/SSTable evidence and establish business deletion authority rather than trusting the largest skewed clock. I reconcile the exact range through the supported bounded path, prove every replica and consumer, then enforce per-range repair-age and outage-to-grace policy.
weakAnswer: Run a full repair, delete the rows again at QUORUM and increase gc_grace_seconds.
whyWeak: It mutates evidence, may overload the cluster, does not prove range or business authority, and changes policy without explaining missed repair, purge or clock risk.

evidence.signal: partition keys tokens and replica set
deletion timestamps outage and clock offsets

followUps.prompt: Why is the green repair job insufficient?
followUps.answer: A global terminal status can hide skipped ranges or tables; deletion safety depends on successful coverage of the affected replicas and range within the horizon.

followUps.prompt: Why not trust the newest timestamp?
followUps.answer: Cassandra's reconciliation timestamp is technical ordering. Clock skew or client timestamps can make an older business event appear newer, so business operation authority must be established independently.
Maximum outage plus repair scheduling delay plus worst measured repair duration plus safety margin must stay below deletion grace, with explicit successful range coverage.
